instruction.first_line: Yes and no: my reputation is systems and culture, but I've owned everything upstream of instruction, and I've led academics directly.
instruction.script:
Yes and no: my reputation is systems and culture, but I've owned everything upstream of instruction, and I've led academics directly. I'm not the person who's going to know the twelfth grade AP government standards cold.

People brought me in to work on behavior, and every time we realized that until operations are stable, it's really hard. You've got thirty kids in a hallway and nobody knows where to go because their schedule is wrong. Operations is **the first line of defense**, so the real rock stars, the teachers and students, can go shine.

And I came up in schools that were about academics. Excel, which was a turnaround. Collegiate, which was high school, special education, a true **all means all** mission. One of our schools, Carver, had the largest CREDO effect size in the country.

At KIPP I led academic health nationally, across forty-eight high schools: GPA, course failures, attendance, and whether a kid feels like they belong. And when I was interim high school principal at Brooklyn Lab, while serving as superintendent, instruction was part of my role. [beat] At KIPP, forty-six percent of ninth graders finished the quarter at a 3.0 or better, up six points. [land] **Best quarter KIPP had ever had** on that number. [STOP]
instruction.landing: Best quarter KIPP had ever had on that number.

lab.first_line: The hardest call I've made was removing the principal at Brooklyn Lab and running the high school myself, because it needed to be done.
lab.script:
The hardest call I've made was removing the principal at Brooklyn Lab and running the high school myself, because it needed to be done.

I came in as transition superintendent. The founder was trying to exit, the schools were being transferred to new ownership, and we had two renewals coming at the same time. Then COVID. We didn't have strong systems in place, and frankly, we didn't have **a team that really trusted each other**.

So I made the call. I removed the principal and served as interim high school principal for half a year, while serving as superintendent. [beat] I did not spread myself evenly across three schools, because **that's how you fail everything on time**.

And the stakes were real. A charter renewal isn't a project deadline. Missing it doesn't mean late. It means the school doesn't exist next year. Now do that twice at the same time. [slow] We built a remote school, we led through COVID, and we got through both renewals. [land] Both schools were reauthorized. [STOP]

leftkipp.first_line: I left because the work was done: we built a national high school strategy, passed it back to the regions, and it's working.
leftkipp.script:
I left because the work was done: we built a national high school strategy, passed it back to the regions, and it's working. I was brought on for One KIPP to design, launch, pilot and refine it.

What I want next is **a small group of people solving the problems within arm's reach**. That's the happiest I've ever been professionally. Since KIPP, I've been building custom AI tools for school leaders, doing school leader consulting, and sales advisory.

The project doesn't end when we run the first full cycle. **It ends when we run that cycle without me.** [beat] Twenty-eight regions, forty-eight high schools. They're running it now. [STOP]
leftkipp.landing: Twenty-eight regions, forty-eight high schools. They're running it now.

assocdean.first_line: My biggest failure was an associate dean I managed: I filed him early as relationships, not systems, and I didn't update my thinking.
assocdean.script:
My biggest failure was an associate dean I managed: I filed him early as relationships, not systems, and I didn't update my thinking.

He was a wonderful human being and a true friend. He was the guy everybody loves. Parents just couldn't get upset with him, and if they did, he found a way to make it work. I'm more on the systems side. That split worked at first, when we were stabilizing the school. But in years three and four, I wasn't developing him to become a Dean of Students.

Then I knew I'd be leaving at the end of the year, and all of a sudden I had six months before he'd be Dean of Students. [beat] **And I realized I'd failed him.**

So I got **crystal clear** about what he was good at and what he needed to develop. It was a little bumpy, but within a month he was clearly meeting well-established targets. If I'd started two or three years earlier, he'd have been much further down the road, and so would the school. [land] He was Dean of Students for many years after, and today he's co-Dean of Students with one of my former students. [STOP]
assocdean.landing: Today he's co-Dean of Students with one of my former students.
